title: Phases in a class of associative memories via hidden neurons
abstract: Associative memory in the Hopfield network is attractor dynamics in a disordered many-body system, and higher-order and exponential extensions turn its retrieval update into softmax attention. The polynomial and exponential regimes have been analyzed by different methods, with no common architecture in which to ask what fixes the storage scale. In this paper we study the bipartite architecture of Krotov and Hopfield, which we call the class $H$, whose model is fixed by a Lagrangian for each layer, taking the hidden neurons as the order parameter of retrieval. At polynomial load the replica method yields the replica-symmetric phase diagrams and closed-form capacities, and the crosstalk moment is common to Ising and spherical visible neurons, so their differences come from the visible entropy. With a softmax hidden layer the load is exponential, and a copy representation maps the thermodynamics onto random-energy-model counting, with paramagnetic, condensed, and frozen phases. Heating destabilizes retrieval by quantized reassignments of attention, and typical Gaussian patterns remain metastable at every load. The regimes differ in their crosstalk statistics, central-limit at polynomial load and large-deviation at exponential load, and the class $H$ splits retrieval into two roles, the visible Lagrangian fixing stability and the hidden one the storage scale, two axes that may also guide the design of new Lagrangians.
summary: This paper develops a unified theoretical framework, the class H, to study associative memories by treating hidden neurons as the order parameter. It analyzes how retrieval dynamics change between polynomial and exponential loading regimes, revealing distinct crossover behaviors in crosstalk statistics. The work provides a deep physical understanding of how stability and storage capacity are governed by separate Lagrangian components.
main_problem: The paper aims to unify the study of associative memory retrieval across different loading regimes (polynomial vs. exponential) by analyzing a generalized bipartite architecture.
main_result: The proposed class H splits retrieval into two distinct roles: the visible Lagrangian controls stability, while the hidden Lagrangian dictates the storage scale and disorder statistics.
method: The analysis employs advanced statistical physics techniques, including the replica method and mapping to random-energy models, to derive phase diagrams and capacities.
model_or_system: The system is the 'class H,' a bipartite network combining Krotov and Hopfield architectures, modeled by an energy function involving visible and hidden neuron dynamics. The hidden neurons are treated as the order parameter for memory retrieval.
key_observables: Retrieval overlap ($m$), Edwards–Anderson order parameter ($q$), and crosstalk noise ($r$).
important_parameters: Load parameter ($\alpha_k$), inverse temperature ($ eta$), and the distinction between polynomial and exponential load regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the replica symmetric (RS) ansatz in the replica method, and the adiabatic limit ($	au_v \gg 	au_h$) is used for certain derivations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the bipartite network structure. Figure 2 shows the RS phase diagram in the $(\alpha_k, T)$ plane, distinguishing retrieval, spin glass, and paramagnetic phases. Figure 5 overlays dynamical escape barriers onto equilibrium phase diagrams.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the model using the replica method for polynomial loads (Models A and C), then extends to exponential loads (Model B). It develops the general framework (class H) and discusses the physical interpretation of the different Lagrangian components.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of statistical mechanics tools (replica method, random-energy models) to neural network dynamics provides deep insights into pattern storage capacity and phase transitions, which are foundational concepts in many-body physics.
